concept.name: Monetary policy
concept.definition: The actions and communications of a central bank to influence the availability and cost of money and credit in pursuit of macroeconomic goals. In the United States, the Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy under its congressional mandate of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.
concept.intuition: It is the economy's thermostat: the central bank tightens to cool demand and inflation, and eases to support growth and employment.
concept.mechanics: The FOMC meets eight times a year to set a target range for the federal funds rate, implemented through open market operations, interest on reserve balances, the discount rate, and reserve requirements. Changes in the funds rate transmit to other short-term rates, foreign-exchange rates, long-term rates, money and credit, and ultimately employment, output, and prices.
concept.failure_modes: Transmission works with long and variable lags, so policy can overshoot; at the zero lower bound conventional rate policy loses traction, forcing reliance on balance-sheet tools and guidance.
concept.misconceptions: The Fed does not set mortgage rates or the money supply directly, and it is legally independent: Congress sets the goals, but the FOMC chooses the instruments and timing.
concept.example: Between March 2022 and July 2023 the FOMC raised the federal funds target range from 0-0.25% to 5.25-5.5%, the fastest tightening cycle since the early 1980s, after CPI inflation peaked at 9.1%.
